source.excerpt: Every time we teach a child something, we keep him from inventing it himself.
trail: Quote Investigator reports checking Piaget’s “Some Aspects of Operations” in Play and Development (1972), p. 27, on paper.
QI distinguishes that genuine wording from the version repeated by Magda Gerber in Dear Parent (1998), p. 12; Gerber may have been paraphrasing rather than offering a verbatim quote.
The inspected WorldCat record corroborates the symposium’s 1972 Norton publication. The original quoted page itself was not inspected here.

author.heading: About Jean Piaget
author.bio: Jean Piaget (1896–1980) was a Swiss psychologist known for research on children’s development and the construction of knowledge. At the University of Geneva he founded the International Center for Genetic Epistemology in 1955; his account of active learning continues to influence education.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Piaget’s cited passage encourages children to experiment and reconstruct understanding for themselves. It also explicitly gives teachers a role in guiding children through suitable materials. The surrounding argument therefore should not be reduced to a blanket instruction never to teach.

schema.claimReviewed: Jean Piaget wrote the exact popular wording “When you teach a child something you take away forever his chance of discovering it for himself.”
schema.faqAnswer: Jean Piaget wrote a similar sentence in 1972 about teaching a child and preventing him from inventing something himself. Quote Investigator finds no substantive support for the exact “take away forever” version, which appears later in Magda Gerber’s writing.
schema.verdictNote: The author of the underlying thought is Piaget; the dispute is exact wording. The source passage also recognizes guidance by teachers.
